strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.119.55	Hebrew z-k-r: remembering the name	The commentary’s ذَكَرَ is “remembered/mentioned”; the psalmist says he remembered the Lord’s name at night and kept the law, a direct Hebrew cognate in a devotional setting.

strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.4.30	king boasts of his own majesty	The commentary identifies Pharaoh’s “highest lord” claim as arrogant self-exaltation; Nebuchadnezzar claims Babylon was built by his own power for the glory of his majesty, making the ruler’s boast explicit.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.4.34	Aramaic title for the Most High	The commentary labels ٱلْأَعْلَى with an elevation root; after his humiliation Nebuchadnezzar blesses the Aramaic “Most High” and praises his everlasting dominion, coupling a related Semitic title with worship.

medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.2.23	Aramaic š-b-ḥ, praise in prayer	The commentary labels سَبِّحِ as tasbih, glorifying God; Daniel thanks and praises the God of his fathers for revealing the king’s secret, using the Aramaic praise cognate in a prayer that credits divine wisdom.

strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.8.36	gaining the world and losing one’s life	The commentary criticizes preferring the low, near life; Jesus asks what it profits someone to gain the whole world and forfeit life, making the choice’s cost explicit.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:2Tim.3.8	Jannes and Jambres oppose Moses	The commentary says Moses’ magicians believe and receive high degrees; Paul names Jannes and Jambres as opponents of Moses who resist the truth, preserving a contrary Christian memory of the magicians.

const content = `strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.34.4\texalt the Lord’s name together\tThe commentary commands praise of the Lord’s high name; in David’s psalm the worshippers are told to magnify YHWH together and exalt his name together, a direct communal formulation.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.113.3\tname praised from sunrise to sunset\tThe commentary joins the Lord’s name to praise; this hymn says the Lord’s name is to be praised from the rising of the sun to its setting, extending the act across the whole day.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.96.8\tglory due the name and offerings in the courts\tThe commentary links raised houses, the Lord’s name, and worship; the psalm tells worshippers to ascribe glory to the Lord’s name and bring an offering into his courts.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Deut.12.5\tchosen sanctuary where God places his name\tThe commentary cites houses authorized for worship with the Lord’s name in them; Deuteronomy commands Israel to seek the place God chooses for his name and dwelling, supplying the covenant sanctuary background.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Exod.20.24\taltar and remembered name\tThe commentary links remembering the Lord’s name with prayer; God says he will come and bless at every altar where he causes his name to be remembered, joining invocation to sacrifice.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Mal.1.11\tgreat name among nations and pure offering\tThe commentary ties praise of the Lord’s name to worship in houses; Malachi says the Lord’s name is great among the nations and that offerings are made to it across the earth.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Neh.9.5\tglorious name exalted above blessing and praise\tThe commentary commands exaltation of the Lord’s name; the Levites’ public prayer blesses God’s glorious name, exalted above all blessing and praise.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Job.1.21\tblessed name in bereavement\tThe commentary defines tasbih as declaring God free of every evil; after losing his children and possessions Job blesses the Lord’s name, showing praise under calamity rather than only in prosperity.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Dan.2.20\tblessed name, kings raised and removed\tThe commentary contrasts God’s true height with a ruler’s claim; Daniel blesses God’s name forever because wisdom and might belong to him and he removes and sets up kings.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Dan.4.17\tMost High rules human kingdoms\tThe commentary’s Pharaoh claims supreme rule for himself; the heavenly decree in Daniel says the Most High rules the kingdom of humanity and gives it to whom he wills, framing Nebuchadnezzar’s later boast and humbling.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Dan.4.31\tkingdom taken during the king’s boast\tThe commentary presents Pharaoh’s “I am the highest lord” as a creature’s false claim; Daniel’s heavenly voice interrupts Nebuchadnezzar’s boast and announces that his kingship has departed from him.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Exod.34.5\tthe Lord descends and proclaims his name\tThe commentary calls for praise of the Lord’s name; at Sinai the Lord descends in a cloud and proclaims the divine name before Moses, giving the naming formula a theophanic setting.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Exod.34.6\tname proclaimed through merciful attributes\tThe commentary defines tasbih as denying every evil of God; the proclamation following the name calls the Lord merciful, gracious, patient, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Num.6.25\tlight of the Lord’s face\tThe commentary’s cited expression about the radiance, majesty, and light of the Lord’s face has a close benediction parallel: the priest asks that the Lord make his face shine upon Israel.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.4.7\tprayer for the light of God’s face\tThe commentary connects the Lord’s face with glory and light; the psalmist prays for the light of God’s face to shine upon the worshippers, making the image explicitly devotional.
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Exod.33.20\tseeing God’s face and the limit of mortal life\tThe commentary cites language about the Lord’s face as overwhelming glory and light; when Moses asks to see God’s glory, Exodus says no human can see God’s face and live, setting a distinct boundary around that face imagery.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Exod.24.17\tglory appearing as devouring fire on the mountain\tThe commentary connects divine majesty and light with the great fire; at Sinai the Lord’s glory appears to Israel like a devouring fire on the mountain’s summit, joining height, glory, and fire.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Deut.4.24\tthe Lord as consuming fire\tThe commentary names the great fire in the judgment scene; Moses warns Israel that the Lord their God is a consuming fire, so the fire image also expresses divine holiness and judgment.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:1Sam.2.1\tHannah’s exaltation and praise\tThe commentary pairs the Lord’s exaltation with a worshipper’s prayer; Hannah says her strength is exalted in the Lord and rejoices in his salvation, placing elevation in grateful devotion rather than self-claim.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:1Sam.2.7\tGod brings low and raises up\tThe commentary makes highness and lowliness opposite ends of one axis; Hannah’s prayer says the Lord makes poor and rich and brings low and raises up.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:1Sam.2.8\tthe needy raised from dust to sit with princes\tThe commentary describes the chosen life as low and lesser; Hannah says God lifts the needy from the dust and seats them with princes, a concrete reversal of low status.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.147.6\tGod raises the humble and casts down the wicked\tThe commentary contrasts true divine elevation with a ruler’s arrogance; the psalm says the Lord raises the humble and casts the wicked down, assigning the upward and downward movement to God.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.75.8\tGod puts one down and lifts another\tThe commentary treats elevation as the Lord’s rightful attribute and worldly self-exaltation as false; the psalm calls God the judge who brings one down and raises another.
medium\ttevrat\tsoydas\tWLC:Job.36.5\tHebrew kabbir and Arabic k-b-r\tThe commentary labels ٱلْكُبْرَىٰ with k-b-r and explains tekbir as declaring God great; Job calls God kabbir, “mighty,” attesting a related Semitic greatness word, though the Hebrew verse emphasizes might.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Zech.14.9\tone king over earth and one name\tThe commentary praises the Lord as highest and links the name to worship; Zechariah says YHWH will be king over all the earth and his name one, uniting universal rule with the divine name.
strong\ttevrat\tsoydas\tWLC:Gen.11.4\tHebrew shem and Arabic ism in the self-made name\tThe commentary labels ٱسْمَ as a name whose mention is raised; Babel’s builders seek to make a shem for themselves while raising a tower toward heaven. Hebrew shem is cognate with Arabic ism, though the Hebrew verse does not derive it from height.
strong\ttevrat\tsoydas\tWLC:Ps.8.2\tHebrew shem and Arabic ism in praise\tThe commentary labels ٱسْمَ as the name that raises the named one’s remembrance; the psalm calls YHWH’s shem majestic throughout the earth. The cognate appears in a praise formula, without importing the commentary’s proposed etymology.
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Isa.14.12\tmorning star fallen from heaven\tThe commentary develops a silhouette rising above the horizon and a ruler’s claimed height; Isaiah addresses a fallen morning star before recounting the speaker’s ascent and boast, adding a celestial image to the self-exaltation scene.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\t1 Enoch 14:20-22\tthrone glory, streams of fire, and unapproachable face\tThe commentary’s gloss connects the Lord’s facial radiance and majesty with light and fire; Enoch’s heavenly throne vision joins fiery streams to overwhelming glory and a face no flesh can behold.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Luke.1.51\tGod scatters the proud\tThe commentary treats Pharaoh’s claim to highest rank as arrogance; Mary’s hymn says God scatters the proud in the intention of their hearts, adding the divine reversal of self-exaltation.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Matt.6.21\ttreasure reveals the heart’s allegiance\tThe commentary says people choose the low and near life; Jesus says the heart follows its treasure, making the preference for earthly life an inward allegiance rather than a mere circumstance.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Matt.6.24\tchoice between God and wealth\tThe commentary names a choice of the lower, nearer life; Jesus says no one can serve both God and mammon, making that preference a direct choice of master.
strong\tincil\tyorum_gelenegi\tSBLGNT:Rom.9.17\tPaul reads Pharaoh’s role as serving God’s name\tThe commentary presents Pharaoh’s “highest lord” claim as false human elevation; Paul quotes Exodus to say Pharaoh was raised up so God’s power and name would be proclaimed, interpreting the same ruler as an instrument of divine sovereignty.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:2Cor.4.6\tGod’s glory shines in Christ’s face\tThe commentary’s gloss joins radiance and light to the Lord’s face; Paul describes the knowledge of God’s glory in the face of Christ, with light shining in human hearts.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:2Cor.4.18\tvisible transient things and unseen eternal things\tThe commentary hears al-dunya as the nearer, lesser life and the surah contrasts it with what lasts; Paul says visible things are temporary while unseen things are eternal.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Luke.9.24\ttrying to save life and losing it\tThe commentary warns that people prefer the low, near life; Jesus says whoever seeks to save life will lose it, while whoever loses life for his sake will save it.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Col.3.2\tset the mind above, not on earth\tThe commentary sets the high against the near earthly life; Paul commands believers to seek the things above rather than things on earth, stating that orientation directly.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Phil.3.19\tearthly-mindedness as the road to destruction\tThe commentary calls the chosen earthly life low and nearer; Paul describes people whose minds are set on earthly things and whose end is destruction, supplying a concrete moral consequence.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Phil.3.20\tcitizenship in heaven\tThe commentary’s axis contrasts the near life with a higher enduring orientation; Paul says believers’ citizenship is in heaven, naming the alternative to earthly-mindedness.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Heb.12.29\tGod as consuming fire in a call to worship\tThe commentary links divine majesty and the great fire; Hebrews urges reverent worship because God is a consuming fire, bringing the image into a Christian liturgical warning.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Luke.10.18\tSatan falls from heaven\tThe commentary sets true divine height against a creature’s arrogant claim; Jesus says he saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning, a specific heavenly fall that resonates with the descent of Isaiah’s self-exalting figure.
